scope.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves and wave graphs

owned_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse and interpret graphical representations of transverse and longitudinal waves

scope.current_boundary: Consolidates legacy lessons l05 and l06. Covers direction-based definition and comparison of transverse and longitudinal waves (oscillations perpendicular or parallel to energy transfer), physical identification of compressions and rarefactions in longitudinal waves, interpretation of displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs, deducing instantaneous particle motion direction from a travelling wave profile, and translating longitudinal waves to displacement graphs using displacement gradients. Strictly excludes wave intensity and amplitude-squared relationships (deferred to 9702_t07_cm04_l07), Doppler effect (deferred to 9702_t07_cm05_l09), electromagnetic spectrum wavelength ranges (deferred to 9702_t07_cm06_l11), full polarisation theory and Malus's law (deferred to 9702_t07_cm07_l13), and stationary waves/interference (deferred to Topic 8).
prior_scope_summaries_consulted: 9702_t07_cm01_l01: Progressive waves transfer energy without net transfer of matter through local oscillations about equilibrium positions.
9702_t07_cm01_l02: Wave quantities defined: displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, wavelength, wave speed, and phase difference.
9702_t07_cm02_l03: Determining amplitude and frequency with a CRO, and deriving and applying the progressive wave equation v = f lambda.
9702_t01: Vectors, scalar versus vector quantities, Cartesian coordinates, and right-angled resolution.

concepts.name: Progressive wave energy transfer and local particle oscillation
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite foundation owned by lesson 9702_t07_cm01_l01; a progressive wave transfers energy through a medium without transferring the matter itself, as particles undergo local oscillations about equilibrium.
misconceptions: Believing that particles travel along with the wave from source to detector.
Confusing the speed of energy propagation with the instantaneous speed of oscillating particles.
demands: Recall that a progressive wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.
Identify that particles of the medium oscillate locally about fixed equilibrium positions.

concepts.name: Wave parameters reminder: displacement, amplitude, wavelength, period, frequency, and wave speed
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite quantities owned by lessons 9702_t07_cm01_l02 and cm02_l03; required to interpret graphs and compute wave properties.
misconceptions: Confusing wavelength (spatial repeat) with period (temporal repeat).
Measuring amplitude from peak to trough rather than from equilibrium to peak.
demands: Recall displacement as distance and direction of a particle from equilibrium.
Recall amplitude, wavelength, period, and frequency f = 1/T.
Recall and apply the wave equation v = f lambda.

concepts.name: Definition and characteristics of transverse waves
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m02_o01 and official definition 9702_def_transverse_wave; tested repeatedly in P2 (9702_m16_22_q04_a_i, 9702_s16_22_q04_a, 9702_m24_22_q05_a).
misconceptions: Classifying a wave as transverse based solely on whether a sinusoidal curve is drawn on paper.
Assuming all transverse waves require a physical material medium (ignoring electromagnetic waves).
demands: State verbatim definition: a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
Identify the two directions to compare: direction of energy transfer and direction of particle oscillation.
Identify physical examples of transverse waves including electromagnetic waves, waves on strings/ropes, surface water waves (predominantly), and seismic S-waves.

concepts.name: Definition and characteristics of longitudinal waves
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m02_o01 and official definition 9702_def_longitudinal_wave; tested across P2 (9702_s16_22_q04_a, 9702_s17_22_q05_b, 9702_w18_22_q04_a, 9702_s19_23_q05_c_i).
misconceptions: Thinking that longitudinal waves push medium particles forward in a continuous stream rather than back and forth about equilibrium.
Believing longitudinal waves cannot be represented by sinusoidal graphs.
demands: State verbatim definition: a wave in which particle displacement is parallel to the direction of energy propagation.
Apply the two-arrow test: show that particle oscillation vector is collinear or parallel to the energy transfer vector.
Identify physical examples of longitudinal waves including sound waves in all states of matter, compression waves along a slinky spring, and seismic P-waves.

concepts.name: Compressions and rarefactions in longitudinal waves
concepts.why_this_depth: Core structural mechanism of longitudinal propagation; directly tested in Cambridge questions (9702_w22_23_q04_a_i, 9702_s21_11_q22, 9702_w21_13_q22, 9702_w16_12_q23).
misconceptions: Believing that compressions are permanent clusters of particles that travel together across the medium.
Measuring wavelength from a compression to the nearest rarefaction instead of to the next compression.
Confusing regions of maximum particle crowding with regions of maximum displacement.
demands: Define a compression as a region where particles are closer together than their equilibrium spacing (higher density/pressure).
Define a rarefaction as a region where particles are farther apart than their equilibrium spacing (lower density/pressure).
Recognise that compressions and rarefactions travel through the medium at wave speed while individual particles oscillate locally.
Determine spatial intervals: center of compression to center of next compression is one wavelength lambda; center of compression to nearest rarefaction is lambda / 2.

concepts.name: Displacement-distance graph as a spatial snapshot and determination of wavelength
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m02_o02; tested across P2 (9702_m16_22_q04_c, 9702_s24_23_q04_a_c, 9702_w22_23_q04_a).
misconceptions: Reading the period of a wave from the horizontal axis of a displacement-distance graph.
Treating a displacement-distance curve as the trajectory traced by a single moving particle over time.
demands: Interpret a displacement-distance graph as an instantaneous snapshot of all particles along the wave at a single fixed instant in time.
Determine amplitude as the maximum displacement from the equilibrium line.
Determine wavelength lambda as the horizontal distance between consecutive points in identical phase of oscillation (e.g. crest to crest).
Recognise that the distance between consecutive points in antiphase is lambda / 2.

concepts.name: Displacement-time graph as a single-position history and determination of period
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m02_o02; essential for distinguishing time-domain traces from spatial wave profiles.
misconceptions: Reading the wavelength of a wave from the horizontal axis of a displacement-time graph.
Assuming that a displacement-time graph shows the spatial shape of the medium across a room.
demands: Interpret a displacement-time graph as the oscillation history of one single particle at a fixed position as time elapses.
Determine amplitude as the maximum displacement from equilibrium.
Determine period T as the time interval between consecutive identical oscillation states.
Calculate frequency f = 1/T from the graph and use it with wave speed v to deduce wavelength via lambda = v/f.

concepts.name: Contrasting distance and time representations and rejecting literal particle trajectory
concepts.why_this_depth: Directly targets the central graph-reading error where students conflate spatial profiles with temporal traces.
misconceptions: Assuming that identical sinusoidal curves must represent identical physical phenomena without checking the axes.
Believing that any sinusoidal curve represents a transverse wave.
demands: Execute the mandatory three-step graph interpretation routine: (1) read both axes, (2) extract values, (3) link to wave physics.
Demonstrate that two identical sinusoidal waveforms represent completely different physical records depending on whether the horizontal axis is distance (x) or time (t).
Explain that a graph is an abstract plot of displacement values and not a photographic path of particle motion.

concepts.name: Determining instantaneous particle motion direction from a travelling wave profile
concepts.why_this_depth: Major discriminator on Cambridge P2 examinations (9702_s24_23_q04_b, 9702_w22_23_q04_a_iii).
misconceptions: Assuming that particles at positive displacement (above the axis) must be moving upward and particles at negative displacement must be moving downward.
Believing particles at crests or troughs are moving with maximum velocity (rather than being instantaneously at rest).
Drawing the velocity arrow in the direction of wave travel (e.g. horizontally to the right for a transverse wave).
demands: Apply the wave profile shift technique: sketch the profile shifted by a small distance delta_x in the direction of wave travel.
Compare the new displacement to the original displacement at the chosen position to determine particle velocity direction.
Deduce that for a wave travelling to the right, a point on a positive/upward slope moves downward, while a point on a negative/downward slope moves upward.
Recognise that particles at wave crests and troughs have momentarily zero velocity.

concepts.name: Interpreting longitudinal displacement-distance graphs and connecting displacement gradient to particle crowding
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m02_o02 and resolves a classic high-error question type in Cambridge physics (9702_w22_23_q04, 9702_s21_11_q22, 9702_s18_11_q22).
misconceptions: Labeling a displacement peak as a compression and a displacement trough as a rarefaction.
Assuming that zero displacement means zero pressure change or normal particle spacing.
Failing to account for the assigned sign convention (e.g. positive displacement = rightward shift).
demands: Identify that for a longitudinal wave, the vertical axis plots scalar displacement along the line of wave travel (positive = right, negative = left).
Translate displacement values into physical particle positions: positive displacement shifts particle rightward, negative shifts it leftward.

Deduce that at a downward zero-crossing (negative gradient), particles to the left are shifted right (+x) and particles to the right are shifted left (-x), crowding particles together to form a compression.

Deduce that at an upward zero-crossing (positive gradient), particles to the left are shifted left (-x) and particles to the right are shifted right (+x), spreading particles apart to form a rarefaction.
Explain why particles at displacement peaks and troughs experience zero displacement gradient, corresponding to normal equilibrium particle spacing and density.

concepts.name: Polarisation capability as an experimental distinction between transverse and longitudinal waves
concepts.why_this_depth: Directly tested in Cambridge as a diagnostic distinction between wave types (e.g. 9702_s25_23_q05_a); full quantitative treatment deferred to module cm07.
misconceptions: Believing sound waves can be polarised by passing through narrow slits.
Assuming that polarisation is a property of all wave types.
demands: State that polarisation is a phenomenon exclusive to transverse waves.
Explain qualitatively why longitudinal waves cannot be polarised: particle oscillations are already restricted to the single direction of energy travel.
Identify sound waves as unpolarisable because they are longitudinal.

concepts.why_this_depth: Belongs strictly to the immediate next lesson 9702_t07_cm04_l07 (outcome 9702_t07_m01_o07).

concepts.why_this_depth: Belongs strictly to course module cm05, lesson 9702_t07_cm05_l09 (outcomes 9702_t07_m03_o01 and 9702_t07_m03_o02).

hook.historical_investigation: Richard Dixon Oldham (1858-1936) and the analysis of seismic P-waves and S-waves from the Great Assam Earthquake of 1897.
hook.why_this_spine: Provides a compelling, real-world physical puzzle demonstrating that a single earthquake event generates two completely distinct waves travelling through the same rock at different speeds and causing ground oscillations in perpendicular versus parallel directions. This investigation led directly to the proof of Earth's liquid outer core because transverse shear waves cannot propagate through liquids.

verified_facts.fact: On 12 June 1897, the Great Assam Earthquake in northeastern India generated powerful seismic waves recorded on Milne horizontal pendulum seismographs across Europe, Asia, and Australia.
verified_facts.source: Oldham, R. D. (1899), Report on the Great Earthquake of 12th June 1897, Memoirs of the Geological Society of India, Vol. 29.

verified_facts.fact: In 1900, British seismologist Richard Dixon Oldham analysed seismograms from across the globe and demonstrated that seismic energy arrives in distinct, separated wave trains: a preliminary tremor arriving first (Primary or P-wave), followed by a second distinct pulse (Secondary or S-wave).
verified_facts.source: Oldham, R. D. (1900), On the Propagation of Earthquake Motion to Great Distances, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, Series A, 194, 135-174.

verified_facts.fact: Oldham proved that the preliminary P-waves are longitudinal compressional waves where rock particles oscillate parallel to the wave path, while the slower S-waves are transverse shear waves where rock particles oscillate perpendicular to the wave path.
verified_facts.source: Oldham, R. D. (1900), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A, 194, 135-174.

verified_facts.fact: In 1906, Oldham observed that S-waves completely fail to propagate through Earth's deep interior, creating a vast shadow zone on the opposite side of the globe and providing the first scientific evidence that Earth has a molten liquid outer core that cannot support shear stress.
verified_facts.source: Oldham, R. D. (1906), The Constitution of the Interior of the Earth, as Revealed by Earthquakes, Quarterly Journal of the Geological Society, 62(1-4), 456-475.

verified_facts.fact: In 1909, Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovicic used the travel-time curves of longitudinal P-waves and transverse S-waves from the Pokupsko earthquake to locate the boundary between Earth's crust and mantle (the Moho discontinuity).
verified_facts.source: Mohorovicic, A. (1910), Das Beben vom 8. X. 1909, Jahrbuch des meteorologischen Observatoriums in Zagreb, 9(4), 1-63.

hook.closing_question: How do the relative directions of particle oscillation and energy transfer distinguish longitudinal P-waves from transverse S-waves, and how do we decode these two fundamental wave types from spatial and temporal displacement graphs?

visuals.purpose: Illustrate the historical hook: contrasting longitudinal P-waves (compressional ground oscillation parallel to energy ray) and transverse S-waves (shear ground oscillation perpendicular to energy ray) producing delayed arrivals on a seismogram record.
visuals.why_this_method: Exact schematic representation showing ray path from earthquake focus through geological strata to a surface seismograph, with side-by-side particle motion vectors and seismogram trace.
visuals.observed_features: Diagram split into subterranean propagation and surface seismogram. Ray path travels upwards-rightwards from earthquake focus. For P-wave, double-headed arrow shows rock particle oscillation parallel to ray path; for S-wave, double-headed arrow shows oscillation perpendicular to ray path. Lower panel shows seismograph trace with baseline, sharp first arrival of low-amplitude P-wave, followed after time delta_t by larger-amplitude S-wave.

visuals.purpose: Teach the two-arrow classification routine by contrasting transverse wave motion on a rope with longitudinal wave motion on a helical spring.
visuals.why_this_method: Clean vector schematic showing particle displacement direction relative to rightward energy transfer without confusing graph shapes.
visuals.observed_features: Two comparative physical panels on white background. Top panel (rope): rightward green energy-transfer arrow labelled 'energy propagation', with a red vertical double-headed arrow at a marked rope point meeting at an explicit right-angle square marker labelled 'perpendicular -> transverse'. Bottom panel (spring): rightward green energy-transfer arrow with a red horizontal double-headed arrow collinear with the spring axis labelled 'parallel -> longitudinal'.

visuals.purpose: Illustrate the physical structure of a longitudinal wave, showing alternating compressions and rarefactions in a spring and in an air column.
visuals.why_this_method: Direct physical representation showing variable coil and particle density with dimensional wavelength markers.
visuals.observed_features: Helical spring with tightly bunched coils labelled 'compression (high density/pressure)' and widely separated coils labelled 'rarefaction (low density/pressure)'. Double-headed horizontal arrow across one compression to the next compression labelled 'wavelength lambda'. Double-headed arrow from compression to adjacent rarefaction labelled 'lambda / 2'. Individual coil marked with short back-and-forth oscillation arrow.

visuals.purpose: Contrast displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs directly, highlighting axis reading as the first diagnostic step.
visuals.why_this_method: Side-by-side comparison of two mathematically identical sinusoidal curves having different horizontal axes to reinforce that axes determine physical meaning.
visuals.observed_features: Side-by-side graph comparison. Left graph: vertical axis labelled 'displacement y', horizontal axis labelled 'distance x'; dashed lines from peak to peak dimensioned as 'wavelength lambda'; caption reads 'Snapshot of many particles at fixed time t0'. Right graph: vertical axis labelled 'displacement y', horizontal axis labelled 'time t'; dashed lines from peak to peak dimensioned as 'period T'; caption reads 'History of one single particle at fixed position x0'. Both mark amplitude A from equilibrium to peak.

visuals.purpose: Provide authentic Cambridge Paper 2 evidence showing a transverse wave snapshot and the determination of particle motion direction.
visuals.why_this_method: Authentic examiner diagram from Paper 2 demonstrating how Cambridge assesses instantaneous motion on a travelling wave profile.
visuals.observed_features: A sinusoidal transverse wave profile labelled 'wave' at one instant, travelling left to right as indicated by an arrow labelled 'direction of travel'. A horizontal dashed equilibrium line passes through the oscillation centre. Point R is located at a positive displacement crest; point T is located at an equilibrium zero-crossing on a rising slope. Caption reads 'Fig. 4.1'.

visuals.purpose: Demonstrate the wave profile shift technique for determining instantaneous particle velocity on a travelling wave profile.
visuals.why_this_method: Exact two-state geometric overlay showing wave profile at time t0 and shifted profile at t0 + delta_t to derive velocity direction without memorising sign rules.
visuals.observed_features: Overlay of two identical transverse wave profiles. Solid blue line represents profile at time t0; dashed red line represents same profile shifted slightly rightwards by distance delta_x = v * delta_t. At point on rising slope, vertical downward arrow shows displacement decreases; at point on falling slope, vertical upward arrow shows displacement increases; at crest and trough, vertical displacement is momentarily unchanged (zero velocity).

visuals.purpose: Provide authentic Cambridge Paper 2 evidence showing discrete particles in a longitudinal wave aligned directly with a sinusoidal displacement-distance graph.
visuals.why_this_method: Authentic examiner diagram from Paper 2 showing exact alignment of particle crowding with graph features.
visuals.observed_features: Horizontal row of 14 discrete particle dots in a medium at time t0 aligned via vertical dashed extension lines with a lower sinusoidal displacement-distance graph. Direction of wave travel arrow points right. A downward-sloping zero-crossing on the graph aligns exactly with closely bunched particles at X (compression). An upward-sloping zero-crossing aligns with widely spaced particles at Y (rarefaction). Particle Z is located between a compression and a rarefaction. Vertical axis labelled displacement, horizontal axis labelled distance. Caption reads 'Fig. 4.1'.

visuals.purpose: Demystify the peak-equals-compression misconception by explicitly translating longitudinal displacement values into physical particle positions.
visuals.why_this_method: Three-tier construction diagram showing equilibrium grid, displacement graph, and displaced grid to prove mathematically why compressions occur at negative-slope zero crossings.
visuals.observed_features: Three vertically aligned horizontal tiers. Top tier: 13 equally spaced dots representing undisturbed equilibrium particles. Middle tier: sinusoidal displacement-distance graph with positive displacement defined as rightwards (+x) and negative as leftwards (-x). Bottom tier: displaced particle dots showing actual positions. Vertical callouts prove that at downward zero-crossing, left particle moves right and right particle moves left, converging into a compression; at upward zero-crossing, left particle moves left and right particle moves right, diverging into a rarefaction; at crest and trough, neighbouring particles shift equally, maintaining normal spacing.

activities.reasoning_step: Classifying various wave types (seismic P-waves, seismic S-waves, ultrasound in tissue, visible light in vacuum, microwaves, plucked guitar string) using the two-arrow test of oscillation direction relative to energy transfer.
misconceptions_addressed: Classifying a wave as transverse because it is drawn as a wavy curve on paper.
Assuming that all longitudinal waves travel at the speed of sound in air.
Believing that light waves require a medium like sound waves.

activities.reasoning_step: Identifying compression centers, rarefaction centers, and calculating wavelength or fractional wavelength intervals on a diagram of unevenly spaced particles or a helical spring.
misconceptions_addressed: Taking the distance from a compression to the nearest rarefaction as one full wavelength lambda instead of lambda / 2.
Believing compressions are physical packets of matter travelling through the medium.

activities.reasoning_step: Discriminating between displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs by reading axes, extracting amplitude, wavelength lambda, or period T, and computing wave speed or frequency.
misconceptions_addressed: Extracting period from a distance axis or wavelength from a time axis.
Treating a displacement graph as the literal flight trajectory of an individual particle.

activities.reasoning_step: Applying the wave profile shift technique to determine the instantaneous direction of particle velocity (up, down, or momentarily at rest) at marked points on a travelling transverse wave profile.
misconceptions_addressed: Assuming particles above the equilibrium axis must be moving upward.
Assuming particles at wave crests have maximum velocity rather than zero instantaneous velocity.
Drawing velocity arrows pointing horizontally in the direction of wave travel.

activities.reasoning_step: Translating a sinusoidal displacement-distance graph of a longitudinal wave into physical medium density states, identifying compressions, rarefactions, and equilibrium density regions using displacement gradients.
misconceptions_addressed: Assuming a displacement crest corresponds to a compression and a displacement trough corresponds to a rarefaction.
Assuming zero displacement implies zero density change.
Failing to apply sign conventions consistently to particles on either side of zero-crossings.

activities.reasoning_step: Evaluating the physical distinction between transverse and longitudinal waves based on polarisation capability, energy transfer, requirement of a material medium, and applicability of v = f lambda.
misconceptions_addressed: Believing that longitudinal sound waves can be polarised.
Assuming that longitudinal waves do not obey the wave equation v = f lambda.

unresolved.resolution: Strictly demarcated by scope boundary: this lesson plans and teaches progressive transverse and longitudinal wave definitions, compressions/rarefactions, and graphical interpretations. Intensity is owned by 9702_t07_cm04_l07; stationary waves and interference are owned by Topic 8 (9702_t08). In worked examples and activities, only the progressive wave classification and graph parts are taught.

unresolved.issue: Polarisation is introduced only as a diagnostic wave-type distinction without quantitative treatment
unresolved.impact: Students might expect coverage of polarising filters, transmission axes, or Malus's law calculations upon encountering polarisation.
unresolved.resolution: Strictly declared in scope boundary: polarisation is mentioned solely as qualitative physical evidence that a wave is transverse (since longitudinal oscillations cannot be polarised, as tested in 9702_s25_23_q05_a). Full treatment of polarisation, polarising filters, and Malus's law belongs to 9702_t07_cm07_l13.
